name: Accounting for Decentralised Treasuries
title: Accounting for Decentralised Treasuries
answer: Accounting for decentralised treasuries covers the recording, measurement and reporting of assets held and controlled by a protocol, a DAO or a similar on chain entity rather than by a conventional company. It sits inside digital asset accounting and borrows from fund accounting, treasury operations and custody practice. The work spans token holdings, stablecoin balances, staked positions, liquidity provided to pools, and the obligations a treasury owes to its token holders or members. It also covers the governance records that show who authorised a transfer and under what mandate.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Accounting for decentralised treasuries covers the recording, measurement and reporting of assets held and controlled by a protocol, a DAO or a similar on chain entity rather than by a conventional company. It sits inside digital asset accounting and borrows from fund accounting, treasury operations and custody practice. The work spans token holdings, stablecoin balances, staked positions, liquidity provided to pools, and the obligations a treasury owes to its token holders or members. It also covers the governance records that show who authorised a transfer and under what mandate.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The records live on public blockchains, so the primary evidence is transaction data rather than a bank statement. Teams read that data through node providers and indexers, then reconcile it against exchange statements, custodian reports and internal ledgers. Wallet addresses, contract addresses and block references act as the account numbers and receipt numbers of the system. Pricing comes from market data feeds, and the choice of feed and timestamp materially changes the numbers a treasury reports.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners map each wallet and contract to an accounting entity, then classify holdings by purpose, such as operating funds, reserves or treasury tokens. They value positions at the reporting date, translate where needed, and record gains, losses, staking rewards and fee income according to the policy the entity has adopted. Reconciliation is continuous rather than monthly, because balances move with every block. Because no single standard governs the area, most teams document their own policy and apply it consistently.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Control is the central question, since a treasury may be managed by a multisignature wallet, a voting process or a small set of key holders. Auditors look for evidence of authorisation, segregation of duties and key management, and for a clear record of who could move funds and when. Provenance matters too, because tokens can arrive from airdrops, bridges or counterparties with unclear history. Disclosure of custody arrangements, related party holdings and any restrictions on tokens is expected, and the site's 229 compliance and regulation pages show how quickly the surrounding rules are still forming.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more standardised on chain reporting, with tagged wallet structures, machine readable disclosures and audit trails that a third party can verify directly. Regulators are moving on custody, reserve and disclosure requirements, which will push treasuries toward the same controls expected of traditional funds. Tooling is consolidating around continuous reconciliation and real time valuation. The open question is how much of the work can be automated before judgement about control and intent still has to be made by a person.
